passage:
Faculty mentor's note, second-year electronics. Wasim.
Suraj came for his mid-semester review today. Marks fine, attendance fine, but he says he 'drags himself' to lab. When I asked why electronics, he was honest: 'My father's shop closed two years ago. I want a job that doesn't disappear.' That's a real reason, and I told him so.
Then I mentioned I'd heard him on tabla at the cultural night. His whole face changed. He talked for ten minutes about a rhythm cycle he's composing, hands tapping the desk.
He isn't choosing wrongly; he's pulled two ways, and the pull is draining him.
Next steps: I suggested the audio signal processing elective next term and told him about the college's recording room. We'll meet again after exams to see where his energy goes.

qa.q: What instrument did Wasim hear Suraj play at the cultural night?
qa.a: The tabla.

qa.q: Why did Suraj choose electronics, and what does his face at the mention of tabla suggest?
qa.a: Suraj wants a secure job after his father's shop closed, a real need; but his face changing and his hands tapping suggest music is what truly excites him.

qa.q: Which of Wasim's choices respects both of Suraj's motives, and why?
qa.a: Suggesting the audio signal processing elective and the recording room; it keeps the secure path while giving music a place, which may bring back some energy.

qa.q: How might Suraj's father see this tension if he knew about it?
qa.a: His father might be relieved that Suraj chose security after the shop closed, yet sad to learn that his son drags himself to lab while lighting up for music.

grounding: A mentor notes a student who chose electronics for job security while drawn to music, with both motives real and the tension draining his energy.

passage:
Thursday
Surveying practical in the sun from nine to one. I measured the wrong baseline twice and Rubina had to redo it. My head was full of the tune I started on Monday.
Here's the thing I don't say out loud: I'm not sorry I took civil. Abbu's salary won't stretch forever, the placement numbers are good, and I like knowing I'll be able to pay Ammi's rent one day. That's real. That matters to me.
But tonight I finished the second verse on Rubina's old keyboard, and it felt as if the whole day had been waiting for that one hour.
Rubina said, 'Sehar, you're two different people. One of them is very sleepy.'
She's right. I don't know how to be both yet. Maybe I don't have to pick. Maybe I just have to stop pretending one of them doesn't exist.

qa.q: What did Sehar finish on Rubina's old keyboard?
qa.a: The second verse of the tune started on Monday.

qa.q: Why does Sehar say 'I'm not sorry I took civil' while dreaming of music?
qa.a: Sehar genuinely values security, helping Abbu and Ammi and getting a good placement; that and the love of songwriting are both real, which is why the day feels split.

qa.q: What choice is Sehar starting to make at the end, and why might it help?
qa.a: To stop pretending the music side doesn't exist instead of picking one; admitting both motives could let Sehar plan time for music and bring more energy to civil too.

qa.q: How does Rubina see Sehar's two sides?
qa.a: Rubina sees 'two different people', a sleepy one in surveying and a lively one at the keyboard, and has had to cover the mistakes; she notices the tension clearly.

grounding: A student in civil engineering for security admits a real pull toward songwriting, and both motives shape how much energy each day gets.

passage:
At the Saturday gardening club in the community centre, the coordinator handed each child a small watering can. Yogesh, six, didn't move. 'What do I get?'
Swati felt her face heat. At home it was the same: 'What do I get?' before putting his shoes away, before feeding the cat. She had started the sticker chart herself, back in March.
The coordinator smiled kindly. 'Here, the tomatoes are the prize. Wait and see.'
Swati knelt beside him. 'Last week you planted that one, remember? Look, it has a flower now. Because you watered it.'
Yogesh peered at the yellow flower. He watered it very carefully, then the next pot too, without asking anything.
That night Swati took the sticker chart off the fridge, keeping one sticker only for really hard jobs. At bedtime she said, 'You helped the tomato grow today.' Yogesh grinned. 'Tomorrow too.'

qa.q: What did Swati take off the fridge that night?
qa.a: The sticker chart, keeping one sticker only for really hard jobs.

qa.q: Why did Swati feel her face heat when Yogesh asked 'What do I get?'
qa.a: She recognised the question from home, asked before every small chore, and realised her own sticker chart had taught him to expect a prize; she felt embarrassed.

qa.q: Which of Swati's choices at the club worked, and why?
qa.a: Showing Yogesh the flower on the tomato plant he had watered; noticing what his effort had done gave the task its own meaning, and he kept watering without asking.

qa.q: How might the coordinator see children like Yogesh asking for prizes?
qa.a: The coordinator seems calm and used to it, trusting that the tomatoes themselves will become the reward once the children watch things grow.

grounding: A parent notices her child asks for a prize before every task and shifts toward pointing out what his effort achieves, keeping rewards rare.

passage:
Dear Sarika,
You asked how the 'chore money' plan is going. Badly, and it's my fault.
Remember I started paying Meenu two rupees for every job? Now she won't fold a towel without asking, 'How much?' Yesterday Paati dropped a whole box of rice, and Meenu stood there and asked if picking it up counted.
That one stung. So I'm trying something different. No money for everyday jobs. Instead I tell her exactly what I noticed: 'You matched every sock; that saved me ten minutes.' 'You helped Paati, and she smiled.' Pocket money stays, but it isn't tied to jobs.
Day three: she laid the table tonight without being asked and said, 'I did it because Paati was tired.'
I almost cried into the dal.
Love,
Lavanya

qa.q: How much did Lavanya pay Meenu for each job?
qa.a: Two rupees for every job.

qa.q: Why did Meenu's question about the rice sting Lavanya?
qa.a: It showed Lavanya that the payments had turned even helping Paati with a mess into a deal; Lavanya felt the plan had pushed out Meenu's own wish to help.

qa.q: What change did Lavanya choose, and why does it seem to work?
qa.a: Stopping payment for everyday jobs and naming exactly what Meenu did and why it mattered; Meenu has started helping for reasons of her own, like Paati being tired. 🙂

qa.q: How might Paati have felt when Meenu asked if picking up the rice counted?
qa.a: Paati might have felt a little hurt or amused at being treated as a paid job, and much warmer later when Meenu laid the table because Paati was tired.

grounding: A parent writes that paying for chores made their child ask 'how much?' each time, and switches to noticing effort and meaning.

passage:
Ramesh, you asked how I survive the warehouse. Honestly? Some nights I don't. Ten hours of scanning barcodes, beep, beep, twelve hundred parcels. Nobody takes that job for love. I take it because of rent.
But around my third month, something shifted. I started noticing where the boxes were going. A lot were headed to small towns in Vidarbha, near my Nani's village. Books, school shoes, a sewing machine once. Somebody out there waiting, the way Nani used to wait for our parcels at Diwali.
The second thing: I asked the supervisor to teach me the inventory system. 'Jatin, you've got a knack,' the supervisor said. Now I'm the one who fixes mismatches. That's a skill. That goes on my CV.
It's still boring, Ramesh. The pay still matters most. But now there's something to hold on to at three in the morning.

qa.q: How many parcels does Jatin scan in a night?
qa.a: Twelve hundred.

qa.q: Why does noticing the parcels' destinations matter to Jatin?
qa.a: It connects the dull scanning to something Jatin values, people in small towns like Nani's waiting for things, so the work feels as if it reaches someone.

qa.q: Which choice helped Jatin most, and why?
qa.a: Asking the supervisor to teach the inventory system; building a real skill for the CV gives the boring hours a purpose beyond pay.

qa.q: How might the supervisor see Jatin's request to learn the inventory system?
qa.a: The supervisor probably sees a worker who cares more than most, and gains someone reliable to fix mismatches, which may open doors for Jatin.

grounding: An adult in a paid but joyless warehouse job finds parts that link to what they value and a skill they are building, which steadies effort without replacing the pay.

passage:
I'm Suraj. I sit opposite Naveen at the accounts office in Coimbatore. For months he typed supplier invoices into the system, eight hours a day, eyes dull. At lunch he'd say, 'Money's money,' and nothing else.
Around June he changed a little. He started keeping a notebook of the errors he found, and wrote himself small formulas to catch them faster. One day he showed me: 'Three hundred wrong entries caught this month. That's three hundred small suppliers who get paid right.'
Once he stayed late to teach his formulas to the new girl on our team.
He still complains about the job. He still says the salary is why he's here. But he doesn't stare through the screen anymore. I don't know exactly what changed in his head. I just know his notebook is almost full.

qa.q: How many wrong entries did Naveen catch that month?
qa.a: Three hundred.

qa.q: What might Naveen's notebook and formulas suggest about how he feels about the work now?
qa.a: They suggest he has found something to care about, a growing skill and making sure small suppliers get paid correctly, even though he still works mainly for the salary.

qa.q: What choice of Naveen's turned a dull task into something steadier?
qa.a: Tracking errors and writing formulas to catch them; it linked the typing to fairness for suppliers and to his own skill, which steadied his effort.

qa.q: How might the new girl Naveen stayed late to teach see him?
qa.a: She might see him as a helpful, skilled colleague rather than someone bored at a screen, and feel welcomed in her first weeks.

grounding: A colleague watches a man in a dull, paid job find meaning in accuracy for small suppliers and a skill he is building.

passage:
Rain drummed on the tin shade, and the school van was already honking at the gate. Yusuf held out Reena's shoes. 'Quick, Abbu will do it.'
'NO. Me do it.' Reena sat on the step and pushed the left shoe onto the right foot. Took it off. Tried again. Her tongue poked out.
Yusuf looked at the clock and breathed out. He crouched and held the shoe still, just still, while Reena pushed her foot in.
She stood up, stamped both feet and beamed. 'I did it!'
They ran through the puddles to the van, two minutes late.

qa.q: What was the weather while Reena put on her shoes?
qa.a: Rain was drumming on the tin shade.

qa.q: Why did Reena shout 'Me do it'?
qa.a: She badly wanted to do it herself; managing her own shoes made her feel big and capable, even with the van honking.

qa.q: What choice did Yusuf make that helped, and why did it work?
qa.a: Instead of taking over, he held the shoe still while Reena pushed her foot in; she still did it herself, and they were only two minutes late.

qa.q: What would change for Reena if Yusuf had just put the shoes on for her?
qa.a: They might have caught the van on time, but Reena would likely have protested and missed that proud 'I did it!' moment.

grounding: A young child insists on putting on her own shoes while the van honks, and her father steadies the shoe instead of taking over.

In the lift lobby of their Pune building, the whole family was ready for Nani's birthday lunch, except for Parveen's shoes. The cab driver had called twice.
'Let me,' said Ujjwal bhaiya, bending down.
'I can DO it!' Parveen pulled the foot away and started on the buckle, missing the hole again and again.
Mumma opened her mouth, then shut it. 'Okay. Buckle's yours. Bhaiya holds the lift.'
Ujjwal held the lift door. Pin, hole, miss. Pin, hole... click.
Parveen looked up, face shining. 'Done! By myself!'
In the cab, Parveen kept swinging both feet to admire the buckles.

qa.q: Who held the lift door?
qa.a: Ujjwal bhaiya.

qa.q: Why did Parveen pull the foot away from Ujjwal bhaiya?
qa.a: Parveen wanted to do the buckle alone; doing it 'by myself' mattered more than being quick.

qa.q: What choice did Mumma make, and why was it a good one?
qa.a: Mumma gave Parveen the buckle and gave Ujjwal bhaiya the lift, so Parveen could finish while the family kept moving.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal bhaiya feel being pushed away when trying to help?
qa.a: He may feel a little brushed off, with the cab waiting, but holding the lift gave him a useful job as well.

grounding: A young child insists on doing a shoe buckle alone while the family is late, and a parent makes room for it.

passage:
Every evening in their house at the edge of a village near Satara, homework time began with a fight. Ritu would drag her slate, sulk and stare at the goats.
One evening Kalyani tried something new. She set two books on the mat, maths and Marathi. 'You choose. Which one first? And do you want to start now, or after we milk the goat?'
Ritu blinked. 'I can pick?'
'You can pick.'
Ritu thought hard. 'Marathi first. Now. Maths after the goat.'
She read her lesson aloud under the bulb without one complaint. After milking, she opened maths herself.
Kalyani said nothing, only smiled into the milk pail. The next evening Ritu was waiting on the mat before she was called.

qa.q: Which subject did Ritu choose to do first?
qa.a: Marathi, straight away, with maths after the goat.

qa.q: Why did Ritu ask 'I can pick?' in surprise?
qa.a: She wasn't used to having any say in homework; being given a real choice surprised her and made her feel trusted.

qa.q: Which choice of Kalyani's changed homework time, and why did it work?
qa.a: Offering two subjects and two times, all still within homework; Ritu felt in charge of her own evening, so the sulking stopped and she started without being told.

qa.q: How might homework time feel different for Kalyani now?
qa.a: Instead of a nightly fight, Kalyani finds a child already waiting on the mat, which likely feels calmer and more hopeful.

grounding: A mother lets her child choose which subject comes first and when to start, and the small real choice brings cooperation.

passage:
In their apartment in Curitiba, Jana used to groan the moment Priscila said the word 'homework'. Most evenings ended with a slammed door.
On Monday Priscila changed her script. She pinned a card to the fridge with two boxes: '4:30, before football' and '7:00, after dinner'. 'Homework happens every day,' she said. 'But you pick when. And you pick which subject goes first.'
Jana narrowed her eyes. 'Any time I want?'
'Either of these two. Your call.'
Jana ticked 4:30 and started with science, because the volcano chapter was fun. By Wednesday she was the one reminding Priscila: 'It's 4:30. I'm doing maths first today. Don't talk to me.'
Priscila hid a smile behind her coffee cup.

qa.q: What two times did Priscila write on the card?
qa.a: 4:30, before football, and 7:00, after dinner.

qa.q: Why was Jana suspicious at first?
qa.a: She was used to homework being ordered, so a real choice seemed too good to be true; she wanted to check how much say she actually had.

qa.q: Which part of Priscila's new plan made the difference, and why?
qa.a: Keeping homework daily but letting Jana choose the time and the first subject; she felt in charge, so she began reminding Priscila herself.

qa.q: How might Priscila feel on Wednesday when Jana says 'Don't talk to me'?
qa.a: Priscila seems amused and relieved, hiding a smile, since the evening fights have turned into Jana owning her homework. 😊

grounding: A parent gives a child two study times and the choice of subject order, and the child starts cooperating on her own.

passage:
Sunaina, you said no to the science camp you begged for, just because I filled in the form. Let me tell you about me at fifteen.
My mother, your Nani, planned my days down to the minute. Wake at 5:30, tuition at seven, school, then painting class at four, 'because you love painting, Nandini'. She even laid out which brushes to take.
And one day I simply refused to go. I loved that class. I'd been saving for new colours. But I sat on my bed and said, 'I'm not going. You can't make me.'
Nani was baffled. So was I, honestly.
It wasn't about painting. It was the only 'no' I had left. When everything is decided for you, even the things you want start to feel like orders.
So, beta. The camp is yours. You fill in the form.

qa.q: What time did young Nandini's painting class start?
qa.a: At four.

qa.q: Why did young Nandini refuse a painting class Nandini loved?
qa.a: With every minute planned by Nani, refusing was 'the only no' left; pushing back protected a sense that some part of life was Nandini's own.

qa.q: What choice does Nandini make for Sunaina at the end, and why?
qa.a: Handing Sunaina the camp form to fill in; giving back ownership makes it easier to want the camp again instead of fighting it.

qa.q: How might Nani have felt when young Nandini refused the class?
qa.a: Nani was baffled; having planned it out of love for Nandini's painting, the refusal probably felt confusing and even hurtful.

grounding: An elder recalls refusing a much-loved class because every step of the day was controlled, and hands the next choice back.

The swimming trials list closed at five, and it was already 4:20. Hrithik had talked about the district team all year.
But that morning Papa had stuck a new timetable on his door: 5:45 wake, 6:00 skipping, 7:00 physics, 'Snack: banana, NOT chips', 4:30 'Go and sign up for swimming trials (Hrithik wants this)'. Every line in Pankaj's neat capitals.
At 4:30 Pankaj knocked. 'Chalo, trials. I'll drive you.'
'I'm not going.'
'What? You've wanted this for months!'
'I said I'm not going.' Hrithik turned the fan up and stared at the ceiling. His chest was tight. He did want it. He just didn't want it to be one more line on Papa's paper.
At 5:02 the sign-up closed. Pankaj sat on the stairs, staring at the timetable, baffled.

qa.q: What time did the swimming trials list close?
qa.a: At five.

qa.q: Why did Hrithik refuse trials he had wanted all year?
qa.a: The trials had become one more line on Papa's timetable; refusing protected Hrithik's sense of owning his own choices, even at the cost of something he wanted.

qa.q: What choice could Pankaj make next time to avoid this standoff?
qa.a: Pankaj could let Hrithik plan his own day and decide about trials himself, offering a lift only if asked; that leaves the wanting with Hrithik.

qa.q: How does the refusal look from Pankaj's side on the stairs?
qa.a: To Pankaj it looks senseless, even ungrateful: he was only helping with what Hrithik wanted, and doesn't yet see the timetable as the problem.

grounding: A teenager whose father scripts every step of his day refuses the trials he wanted, protecting his sense of ownership.

Dear Salma,
Your letter asked if I regret it. Honestly, this semester has been the hardest thing I've done. Fieldwork at six in the heat, blisters, and I failed the soil chemistry mid-term. Papa still tells relatives I'm 'doing some farming course'.
But I don't regret it. Remember my gap year, the four months at the seed bank in Wardha, when I kept a notebook of every question I had? I chose this with that notebook open. Nobody picked it for me.
So when I failed soil chemistry, I didn't think 'why am I here'. I thought 'okay, what didn't I get?' I've been going to the professor's office every Thursday since.
Some batchmates who were sent here by their families have already stopped coming to class. I understand. It's harder to push through for someone else's reasons.
Write back soon,
Kiran

qa.a: At the seed bank in Wardha.

qa.q: Why didn't failing soil chemistry make Kiran ask 'why am I here'?
qa.a: Kiran chose the course after real reflection, notebook of questions open, so the goal feels Kiran's own; a setback became something to fix, not a reason to quit.

qa.q: Which of Kiran's choices after the failed mid-term shows an owned goal at work?
qa.a: Going to the professor's office every Thursday; Kiran treats the failure as a gap to fill, because the reason for being there is personal.

qa.q: How might the batchmates who were sent by their families experience the same hard semester?
qa.a: Without a reason of their own to hold on to, the heat, blisters and failures may feel pointless, which is why some have stopped coming.

grounding: A young adult who chose agriculture after real reflection keeps going through hardship, unlike batchmates pushed into it.

passage:
At the hotel in Amritsar, Baljeet used to love the front desk. He remembered guests' names, suggested quiet times to visit the old bazaar, fixed small problems before they grew.
Then Kiran became shift supervisor. Every email to a guest had to go to Kiran first. Every room change needed a message. Kiran stood behind the desk, reading over his shoulder, changing 'Dear Sir' to 'Dear Guest'.
By the third month Baljeet had stopped suggesting anything. He answered what was asked, logged out on time and drove home too tired to talk.
At the monthly review, his scores had dropped. Kiran asked why. Baljeet said quietly, 'Because nothing I do is mine anymore.'
Kiran was silent for a moment. 'Okay. What matters: complaints closed within your shift, guests leaving happy. How you do it is your call. I'll check results on Friday.'
That week Baljeet stayed late to help a family find a wheelchair for their grandmother.

qa.q: What did Kiran change in Baljeet's emails?
qa.a: 'Dear Sir' to 'Dear Guest'.

qa.q: What did Baljeet mean by 'nothing I do is mine anymore', and how did he feel?
qa.a: With every step checked, he felt drained and untrusted, so he stopped trying anything extra; the work no longer felt like his.

qa.q: What change did Kiran choose at the review, and why did it help?
qa.a: Setting clear outcomes, complaints closed and happy guests, while leaving the method to Baljeet; room for his own judgement brought his initiative back.

qa.q: How might Kiran have seen the constant checking before the review?
qa.a: Kiran probably saw it as careful supervision that prevented mistakes, not realising it was draining Baljeet until the scores dropped.

grounding: A worker whose supervisor checks every step loses energy and does the minimum, until clear outcomes with freedom in method bring initiative back.

passage:
Subject: A request about the grant reports

Dear Irawati,
Thank you for making time on Friday. I wanted to put this in writing so it comes out calmly.
Since March, every paragraph of my grant reports has gone to you before I move to the next one, and I've been asked to share my screen while drafting. I know you want these to be perfect, and so do I.
But I've noticed something in myself. I've stopped thinking ahead. I wait for your edits instead of solving things, and by evening I'm flat. That isn't the worker you hired.
Could we try this for one month: you set what a finished report must include and the deadline, and I send you the full draft two days early? If it misses the mark, we go back to closer checks.
Regards,
Sarika

qa.q: What has Sarika been asked to do while drafting?
qa.a: To share the screen while drafting, and to send every paragraph before moving on to the next.

qa.q: How does Sarika feel about the constant checking, by Sarika's own account?
qa.a: Sarika feels flat by evening and has stopped thinking ahead, waiting for edits instead of solving problems; the initiative has faded.

qa.q: What did Sarika propose, and why is it a sensible trial?
qa.a: Clear requirements and a deadline, with the full draft sent two days early and a return to closer checks if it misses; it gives freedom in method while protecting Irawati's need for quality.

qa.q: How might Irawati feel reading this email?
qa.a: Irawati may feel surprised or a little defensive at first, but the calm tone and the fallback plan make it easier to agree to the trial.

grounding: A micromanaged worker describes how constant checks drained the worker's initiative and proposes clear outcomes with freedom in method.

passage:
At the ghat steps near the temple in their small town, Kamal stood on the second step, knees bent, fists tight. The step below looked very far away.
'Jump, Kamal!' called his didi, Sukanya, holding the flower basket.
He jumped. He landed on both feet, wobbled, and didn't fall. His mouth fell open. 'Didi! I jumped the big one!'
Before she could answer, he climbed back up. Jump. Again. Again. Each time he shouted, 'Did you see?'
Sukanya put the basket down and counted for him. By eleven, the old priest sweeping the steps was counting too.

qa.q: Who was sweeping the steps?
qa.a: The old priest.

qa.q: How can you tell Kamal felt proud after the first jump?
qa.a: His mouth fell open, he shouted 'I jumped the big one!' and climbed straight back up to do it again.

qa.q: What choice of Sukanya's helped Kamal keep practising?
qa.a: She put the basket down and counted his jumps, noticing each one, which fed his pride and his effort.

qa.q: What might the old priest have enjoyed in joining the counting?
qa.a: The priest probably enjoyed Kamal's delight and wanted to share in it, adding another pair of eyes to his proud jumps. 🙂

grounding: A young child proudly jumps a big step and wants to do it again and again, the feeling of being able driving him on.

passage:
The house was full of cousins for Pinky didi's wedding, the dholak going in the courtyard, and Gurpreet sat on the stairs with the fractions worksheet. Third test this month: 3 out of 20. The one before, 5. The one before that, 4.
He tried the first sum again: 2/3 + 1/4. He added the tops and added the bottoms. It looked wrong. It always looked wrong.
Nirmala Aunty, the tuition teacher from next door, came up the stairs with a plate of laddoos. 'Show me where you're stuck.'
Gurpreet folded the worksheet into a tiny square. 'I'm just not a maths person. Everyone knows.'
'Who's everyone?'
He shrugged and went down to the courtyard, where nobody asked about fractions. The folded square stayed on the step.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet score on the third fractions test?
qa.a: 3 out of 20.

qa.q: Why did Gurpreet say 'I'm just not a maths person'?
qa.a: After three failed tests without ever getting better, he has decided the problem is him rather than the method, so trying feels pointless.

qa.q: What choice could Nirmala Aunty make next to rebuild Gurpreet's motivation?
qa.a: She could sit with him on one sum, find the single step that goes wrong, and let him get that step right a few times, so he feels himself improving.

qa.q: How might Nirmala Aunty feel seeing the folded worksheet left on the step?
qa.a: She may feel concerned, seeing that he hasn't just failed fractions but given up on himself, and wonder how to reach him.

grounding: A child who keeps failing fractions decides he is not a maths person and stops trying.

passage:
In Class 6 at the school near Tolichowki, Naveen had stopped even copying down the fraction sums. When Ma'am wrote 3/5 of 20 on the board, he drew a cricket bat in the margin instead.
'Try it,' whispered Wasim, his bench partner.
'What's the point? I got the last four wrong. My brain doesn't do fractions.'
At home in their flat, he left the maths homework for last and then 'forgot' it. Ammi signed the teacher's note in his diary without a word.
On Friday Wasim tried again, cutting his tiffin roti into five pieces. 'Look. Three of these five. Easy.'
Naveen looked at the roti for a second, almost interested. Then he pushed it back. 'For you, maybe.'

qa.q: What did Naveen draw in the margin instead of doing the sum?
qa.a: A cricket bat.

qa.q: What does Naveen's 'For you, maybe' suggest about how he sees himself?
qa.a: It suggests he believes he simply can't do fractions; after four wrong answers, even an easy example feels meant for others, not for him.

qa.q: What was the almost-turning point, and what could help it stick?
qa.a: Naveen looking at the roti slices, almost interested; if Wasim or Ma'am let him solve one very easy sum right then, a small success could start to rebuild his belief.

qa.q: How might Wasim feel when Naveen pushes the roti back?
qa.a: Wasim may feel disappointed after trying twice to help a friend, and unsure how to get through.

grounding: A child who keeps getting fractions wrong concludes his brain cannot do them and stops trying, even when a friend helps.
